title: Minimum-weight triangulation in NP
formal: Does the following language belong to NP? An instance consists of a finite set \(S\subset \mathbb{Q} ^{2}\) of explicitly given points and a rational bound B; it is a yes instance exactly when S has a triangulation whose total Euclidean edge length, counting every edge once, is at most B.
why: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.

progress.text: Strong NP-hardness is proved, while NP membership for exact Euclidean costs remains explicitly unresolved.
Practical exact methods scale to very large tested point sets.
A later primary paper still records the unresolved NP placement of the related square-root-sum comparison problem.

definitions: The input lists \(n\ge 0\) distinct points \((x_{i},y_{i})\), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight \(\mathrm{W}(T)=\sum _{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\sqrt{(x_{i}- x_{j})^{2}+(y_{i}- y_{j})^{2}}\). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality \(\mathrm{W}(T)=B\) is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if \(V(x,y)\) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.

context_blocks.title: The geometry is small; the lengths need not be rational
context_blocks.text: A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points \((0,0), (1,0), (0,1)\) have a single triangular boundary of total length \(2+\sqrt{2}\). A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

context_blocks.title: What a certificate would have to establish
context_blocks.text: The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Hardness is already known
context_blocks.text: Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

context_blocks.title: The related arithmetic frontier
context_blocks.text: An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

context_blocks.title: Large solved instances and worst-case guarantees
context_blocks.text: Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.

sentences: The input gives rational planar points and a rational limit on the total length of a triangulation.
Every input point must be used, no extra points may be added, and Euclidean edge lengths are compared exactly.
The question asks whether every feasible instance has a short certificate that can be checked in polynomial bit time.
NP-hardness is known, but the sum of potentially irrational edge lengths prevents the usual edge-list argument from establishing NP membership.
Practical exact solutions and rounded-cost variants do not settle the certificate question for arbitrary exact inputs.
